--- title: "Fall 2026" date: 2026-09-01 description: "In progress. Part 1: record-warm water off Baja California and the tropical-storm rain of September–October. Part 2: the wettest fall on record, the November 1 atmospheric river, and an El Niño the atmosphere has not yet followed." categories: [In progress] --- Fall here means September–November. This synopsis is being written as the season unfolds. [Part 1](#part-1-warm-water-off-baja-california) covers the warm water off Baja California behind the September–October tropical-storm rain. [Part 2](#part-2-the-wettest-fall-on-record) covers the season's precipitation and temperature against the record, its storms through mid-November, and the atmospheric pattern and ENSO state behind them. ## Part 1: Warm water off Baja California Sea-surface temperatures off Baja California were the highest in the ERSSTv5 record since 1950 for each of July, August and September 2026. Averaged over 18–32°N, 122–108°W (the Pacific side of the peninsula and the Gulf of California), the anomaly relative to 1991–2020 was +1.81 °C in July, +1.90 °C in August, +2.16 °C in September. The previous September record was +1.43 °C in 2015. Over the same period Flagstaff had its two largest rain events of the autumn, [September 27–30](../events/2026-09-27.qmd) and [October 9–13](../events/2026-10-09.qmd). National Weather Service forecasters in Flagstaff attributed the moisture in both to eastern Pacific tropical cyclones: in late September first the remnants of Odalys and then Polo, and in October Rachel (see [What the forecasters said](#what-the-forecasters-said)). The airport recorded 13.25 in from September 1 through November 13, already the 1st largest September–October total of 76 years since 1950. ::: {#789a24fa .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Shading: mean SST anomaly for July–September 2026 relative to 1991–2020 (ERSSTv5). Solid black contour: the 26 °C isotherm in September 2026; dashed: its 1991–2020 September position. Dotted box: the Baja box (18–32°N, 122–108°W). Lines and dots: NHC best tracks of Odalys (dashed), Polo (solid) and Rachel (dotted) (dark red: hurricane; orange: tropical storm; light: tropical depression). ★ Flagstaff.](fall-2026_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {#352ca2d4 .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` July–September mean SST anomaly in the Baja box, 1950–2026 (relative to 1991–2020). 2026 in orange. Hover for each year's value. ::: ::: ### Sea-surface temperature under the storm tracks | Storm | Time (UTC) | Position | Status | Wind (kt) | SST (°C) | 1991–2020 normal (°C) | Difference (°C) | SST month | |:--------|:-------------|:---------------|:---------------|------------:|-----------:|------------------------:|------------------:|:------------| | Polo | Sep 28 12:00 | 23.9°N 113.7°W | hurricane | 100 | 28.3 | 25.2 | 3.1 | Sep | | Polo | Sep 29 00:00 | 25.2°N 112.8°W | hurricane | 100 | 30.4 | 27.7 | 2.7 | Sep | | Polo | Sep 29 12:00 | 26.9°N 111.6°W | hurricane | 65 | 30.4 | 27.7 | 2.7 | Sep | | Rachel | Oct 10 00:00 | 23.3°N 123.6°W | tropical storm | 40 | 23.9 | 22.7 | 1.2 | Oct | | Rachel | Oct 10 12:00 | 24.7°N 120.5°W | tropical storm | 50 | 25.1 | 22.9 | 2.2 | Oct | | Rachel | Oct 11 00:00 | 28.5°N 117.0°W | tropical storm | 55 | 24.7 | 20.9 | 3.9 | Oct | The table lists 12-hourly positions north of 23°N over water. Along them, SST was 23.9–30.4 °C, +1.2 to +3.9 °C relative to normal. Values are monthly means at the nearest 2° ERSSTv5 cell; October positions use September SST, the latest month available. Sea-surface temperatures of about 26 °C or more are generally needed to sustain a tropical cyclone. On the Pacific side of the peninsula, the northernmost September SST of at least 26 °C was at 22°N along 120°W (normal 18°N); 24°N along 118°W (normal 20°N); 26°N along 116°W (normal 20°N) (solid and dashed contours above). The Gulf of California normally exceeds 26 °C in September. Polo was still a 100-kt hurricane at 25°N and a hurricane at 27°N before dissipating over Sonora; Rachel was still a tropical storm at 28.5°N, and its remnant reached southeastern California. Warm water does not steer storms. In both events a trough west of California turned the moisture plume toward Arizona; see the atmospheric setting on the [September 27–30](../events/2026-09-27.qmd) and [October 9–13](../events/2026-10-09.qmd) pages. ### What the forecasters said The National Weather Service office in Flagstaff discussed the moisture source in its Area Forecast Discussions as the event unfolded. Excerpts, quoted verbatim (links to the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive): - **Sep 24, 10:16 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609250516)): "Moisture associated with two tropical cyclones (Hurricane Polo forecast to be off the southern Baja at this time and TS Odalys much farther west) will be pulled northeastward into the southwest United States in advance of this trough." - **Sep 26, 1:23 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609262023)): "Despite the fact the tropical moisture is coming from two tropical cyclones to the south, neither one of these circulations will actually make it up into Arizona." - **Sep 28, 11:43 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609281843)): "Current satellite imagery show a plume of moisture originating from the remnants of Odalys moving across northern Arizona. Meanwhile, Hurricane Polo is centered of the west coast of Southern Baja California." - **Sep 29, 2:03 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609292103)): "Arizona remains under a very dynamic weather pattern today with upper level low pressure centered over western Arizona and moisture from Hurricane Polo streaming northward." - **Sep 30, 2:12 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609300912)): "Water vapor satellite imagery show the upper-level low pressure centered over central Arizona and moving eastward, with moisture from the remnants of Polo now mostly being lifted into eastern New Mexico and western Texas." - **Oct 8, 2:42 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610080942)): "As the trough digs south, it will interact with what will become the remnants of TS Rachel." - **Oct 10, 10:48 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610101748)): "Tropical Storm Rachel, about 500 miles southwest of San Diego as of 8 AM MST, is quickly moving northward as it begins to be pulled northward by an upper-level low off the California coast." - **Oct 11, 3:01 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610111001)): "After making landfall earlier this evening, the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel are moving towards the north- northeast early this morning before exiting into Utah this afternoon. … With a continued strong southerly flow, moisture has continued to advect into the region and have left ripe conditions with the potential for heavy rain through today." - **Oct 11, 11:25 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610111825)): "Moisture from Hurricane Rachel has moved into much of northern Arizona this morning, with PWAT values near or exceeding daily record levels." The forecasters' account matches the ERA5 analysis on the event pages. In the September event, the first surge of moisture was traced by the forecasters to the remnants of Odalys, which stayed west of 123°W and south of 23°N, outside the Baja box; at the time of peak moisture transport over Flagstaff (September 28) ERA5 shows no continuous plume back to Polo. Polo's moisture followed on September 29 as the upper-level low crossed Arizona. In the October event, ERA5 shows the plume over Flagstaff continuous with Rachel at the time of peak moisture transport, and the forecasters reported precipitable water near or above daily records. ### Has warm water off Baja meant a wet autumn before? ::: {#119a7e5c .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![September SST anomaly in the Baja box against Flagstaff airport September–October precipitation, 1950–2025, with a least-squares line. 2026 (orange) uses precipitation reported so far.](fall-2026_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){} ::: ::: - **Correlation, 1950–2025 (n = 76):** r = +0.22 (p = 0.05) between September Baja SST anomaly and Flagstaff September–October precipitation. For comparison, July–September ONI gives r = +0.25. - **Overlap with ENSO:** the Baja box correlates with July–September ONI at r = +0.50. With ONI removed from both, the Baja–precipitation correlation is +0.12 (p = 0.31). - **Warmest fifth of Septembers (n = 16):** 10 were followed by above-median September–October precipitation; their median was 3.65 in, against 3.23 in for all years. The driest of them was 2020, the 3rd warmest September, with 0.05 in. In the record, warm water off Baja has gone with modestly wetter autumns in Flagstaff, and much of that relationship is shared with El Niño. On its own it has not been enough: a wet autumn also needs storms in the eastern Pacific and a pattern that brings their moisture north. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Notes and caveats - **Baseline:** anomalies are relative to 1991–2020. Long-term warming raises recent anomalies relative to earlier decades, so part of 2026's margin over earlier years reflects the trend; 2026 also exceeds the recent record years. - **Resolution:** ERSSTv5 is a 2°, monthly reconstruction. It does not resolve the narrow coastal upwelling zone or day-to-day changes under a storm. - **Precipitation:** Flagstaff airport, threaded station record from RCC-ACIS. The 2026 value is incomplete until October ends. - **Storm tracks:** NHC operational best-track files; final tracks are issued after the season. ::: ## Part 2: The wettest fall on record ### Precipitation and temperature Flagstaff airport recorded **13.25 in** from September 1 through November 13, against a 1991–2020 normal of 3.99 in for those dates (332% of normal). That is already more than any complete September–November in the record since 1899; the previous wettest fall was 1972 with 13.01 in, and the median since then is 4.54 in. Precipitation fell on 26 days, and 4 days had an inch or more: September 29 (1.65 in), October 11 (1.98 in), October 22 (1.01 in), November 1 (3.37 in). November 1 alone brought 3.37 in, the wettest November day in the airport record since 1898 and the 3rd wettest day of any month. The season has also been warm, averaging +2.1 °F against normal, and every storm so far has fallen as rain at the airport. No measurable snow has been recorded there this season, against a normal of 4.1 in by November 13. | Month | Precipitation (in) | Normal (in) | Rank (wettest) | Mean temp. vs normal (°F) | Snowfall (in) | Normal snowfall (in) | |:--------------|:---------------------|:--------------|:-----------------|:----------------------------|:----------------|:-----------------------| | September | 3.50 | 1.84 | 20th of 128 | +2.5 | 0.0 | 0.0 | | October | 6.28 | 1.52 | 2nd of 129 | +1.9 | 0.0 | 1.5 | | November 1–13 | 3.47 | 0.63 | – | +1.4 | 0.0 | 2.6 | *Flagstaff airport (threaded record from RCC-ACIS). Normals 1991–2020. Ranks among all years with a complete month since 1898.* ::: {#0d9b8bb5 .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Cumulative precipitation at Flagstaff airport from September 1, 2026 (orange), the previous wettest falls (1972 and 1985, grey) and the 1950–2025 median (blue).](fall-2026_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ### The storms | Event | Network median (in) | Airport (in) | Peak IVT at Flagstaff (kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹) | Moisture source (NWS Flagstaff) | |:-------------------------------------------|:----------------------|:---------------|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------| | [Sep 23](../events/2026-09-23.qmd) | 0.08 | 0.12 | 68 | Monsoon moisture plume, mostly into New Mexico | | [Sep 27–30](../events/2026-09-27.qmd) | 1.85 | 2.68 | 388 | Remnants of Odalys, then Hurricane Polo | | [Oct 9–13](../events/2026-10-09.qmd) | 3.23 | 3.55 | 490 | Tropical Storm (later Hurricane) Rachel | | [Oct 18–22](../events/2026-10-18.qmd) | 2.24 | 1.84 | 412 | Subtropical plume, partly from post-tropical Trudy | | [Oct 30 – Nov 1](../events/2026-10-30.qmd) | 2.91 | 3.96 | 618 | Subtropical plume from about 24°N; remnant monsoon moisture | *Network median: City of Flagstaff and Coconino County gauges over the event window. Airport: local-day total (the latest day may not yet be reported). Peak IVT: ERA5 at the grid point nearest Flagstaff. Moisture source: as described in NWS Flagstaff Area Forecast Discussions, quoted on each event page.* **October 30 – November 1** was the season's largest storm. It came in two rounds: a shortwave trough with thunderstorms on October 30, then, after a lull, an [atmospheric river](../events/2026-10-30.qmd) ahead of a deep trough that came ashore in central California. Across the city network the median total was 2.91 in (range 1.81–7.64 in), and the airport's 3-day total was 3.96 in, the 3rd largest 3-day total ending in November since 1898. IVT over Flagstaff peaked at 618 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ from the SSW early on November 1, about 2.5 times the atmospheric-river threshold. 89% of the network rain fell while IVT was at atmospheric-river strength. At the peak a closed 500-hPa low was centred at 38.5°N 122.5°W, with 35 m s⁻¹ southwesterly flow at 500 hPa over Flagstaff. SNOTEL gauges caught 1.8 in at Fort Valley, 6.1 in at Snowslide Canyon, 5.1 in at Fry. The storm fell on soils already saturated by the October rain. NWS Flagstaff reported stream gauges above record stage south of the Mogollon Rim and a record flood stage on the Little Colorado River at Winslow. Snow levels stayed high: the airport's lowest temperature during the storm was 34 °F, and overnight lows averaged +12 °F against normal. A smaller storm was still under way on November 13–14 as this was written. It will get its own event page once it is over and ERA5 covers it. ### The pattern: a Gulf of Alaska ridge and a run of cut-off lows The monthly means do not show a persistent West Coast trough behind these storms. In October the 500-hPa height anomaly over the Gulf of Alaska was +71 m (the 8th highest October of 77 since 1950; September: +67 m, 7th highest), with sea-level pressure +5.6 hPa against normal. Off California, the October anomaly was only -1 m in the box most closely tied to Flagstaff winter precipitation (the Southwest trough index on the [Pacific page](../pacific.qmd)). Over the Southwest itself heights were above normal (+33 m in October, +24 m in September), which matches the warm temperatures. Instead, the rain came from individual troughs that broke off south of that ridge as cut-off lows. Between October 1 and November 8, ERA5 had a closed 500-hPa low within 25–42°N, 132–112°W (off California and over the Southwest) in 84 of 156 six-hourly analyses (54%). Cut-off lows move slowly. Each one west of California set up deep southerly flow that carried subtropical and tropical-cyclone moisture from the warm water off Baja (Part 1) north into Arizona, and the ridging between lows gave the dry, mild spells. This describes the season only: the frequency of such lows in other falls has not been computed here. ::: {#f814e57e .cell .column-page execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Sea-surface temperature (ERSSTv5), sea-level pressure and 500-hPa height (ERA5) anomalies for October 2026 and September–October 2026, relative to 1991–2020. H marks the North Pacific High centre. ★ Flagstaff.](fall-2026_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ### El Niño and the negative PDO - **El Niño is strong and still growing.** The August–October ONI was +2.46 °C, the highest for those months since 1950 (previous highest: +2.04 °C in 1997). Monthly Niño 3.4 (ERSSTv5) reached +3.06 °C in October. - **The North Pacific has not followed.** The PDO was -2.26 in October (September–October mean -1.89), lower than 91% of Octobers since 1950, whereas the PDO is usually positive during a strong El Niño. The PNA was +0.28 in October. The Aleutian Low was -2.3 hPa against normal in October, after running weak in August–September. The Gulf of Alaska ridge is the opposite of the deep Aleutian Low and West Coast trough of a canonical El Niño winter. - **The ocean resembles past strong El Niños; the atmosphere does not.** Against the mean of the strong El Niño years (1965, 1997, 2015, 2023) for the same months, the September–October 2026 SST anomaly pattern over the North Pacific matches closely (pattern correlation +0.84), but the 500-hPa height anomaly pattern does not (-0.10). - **El Niño and fall rain in the record.** August–October ONI correlates with Flagstaff September–November precipitation at r = +0.31 (p = 0.007, n = 76). In the 10 falls with ONI ≥ 1.0, 7 were wetter than the median, and their median was 7.85 in, against 4.79 in for all falls since 1950. The one earlier fall with a comparable mismatch (ONI ≥ 1.0 with a September–October PDO ≤ −1.0) is 2023 (ONI +1.5, PDO -2.6). That fall was dry at Flagstaff (2.19 in), and the following November–March brought 10.13 in against a median of 8.67 in. This fall's rain fits El Niño only indirectly. The warm eastern Pacific fed an active hurricane season (Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Trudy and Vance) and the record-warm water off Baja that supplied the moisture. The lift came from cut-off lows under a Gulf of Alaska ridge, not from the extended Pacific jet and deep Aleutian Low that El Niño usually brings in winter. The main question for the coming months is whether that winter response develops or the negative PDO keeps the ridge in place. One comparable year is little to go on: 2023 had the same mismatch, a dry fall and then a winter wetter than the median. The [Pacific page](../pacific.qmd) tracks this monthly. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Notes and caveats (Part 2) - **Season to date:** the latest days of the airport record are provisional, and November is incomplete. The comparison with complete falls uses every year from 1899 with at least 90% of days reported. - **Cut-off lows:** a closed low is a 500-hPa height minimum over a 5° neighbourhood in 6-hourly ERA5 (0.25°), the same test used on the event pages. Shallow lows and open troughs are not counted. - **ENSO and PDO:** ONI and PNA from CPC; PDO from NCEI (ERSSTv5). Strong El Niño years are those with August–October ONI ≥ 1.5. Pattern correlations are over the Pacific page's North Pacific domain. - **Moisture sources:** taken from the forecasters' discussions, which are written in real time; the event pages compare them with ERA5 where it is available. :::
